name: Alsea
status: Four actual-content historical works; one renewed existing source and three new works proposed

sources.title: Alsea Subagency of Siletz Reservation
sources.author: David G. Lewis
sources.annotation: Substantive account of the multi-people subagency, land reductions, removal and descendant communities. Its administrative labels must be separated from Alsea identity. Use the 1865 executive-order chronology rather than repeating the article's congressional attribution.

sources.title: Opening the Coast Reservation: the Oyster Harvest Rush 1863–1866
sources.publisher: The Quartux Journal / Critical Indigenous Perspectives
sources.author: David G. Lewis
sources.annotation: Connects settler intrusion at Yaquina with mining rumors, commercial oyster harvesting and pressure to open reservation land. Useful for the economic setting of Alsea-area displacement, with the broader multi-people Coast Reservation scope retained.

sources.title: Oral Histories of Native Experiences at Yahaats Sub-Agency
sources.publisher: The Quartux Journal / Critical Indigenous Perspectives
sources.author: David G. Lewis; named witnesses in an abridged 1931 Coos claims transcript
sources.annotation: Lewis presents abridged Coos claims testimony about Yahaats within the Alsea reservation system. Witnesses distinguish their experiences, movements and knowledge. This is direct shared-institutional history, not Alsea-authored testimony or a statement of Alsea cultural practices.
sources.scopeClassification: Shared reservation-system context; witnesses largely concern Coos communities

sources.title: Congressional Record, February 20, 1875: Alsea and Siletz reservation amendment debate
sources.author: United States Senate; remarks and proposal by Senator John H. Mitchell, with other senators
sources.annotation: Selected Senate debate exposes the proposal's removal and settlement-opening language and Mitchell's cost-saving rationale. It records legislative argument and procedural decisions, not affected communities' consent or an independently inspected final enactment.

claimBlocks.suggestedSection: A people and an administrative institution
claimBlocks.text: The Alsea Subagency was a federal administrative institution, rather than another name for all Alsea people. David Lewis describes its officials managing Alsea, Siuslaw, Lower Umpqua, Coos and Coquille communities. Its later closure therefore affected several distinct peoples. His account also follows people who moved to Siletz and others who remained in off-reservation homelands; closure of the institution did not mean disappearance of its former residents or their descendants.

claimBlocks.suggestedSection: Resource pressure and loss of reservation land
claimBlocks.text: Lewis's oyster-rush study places reservation reduction within a struggle over resources. Miners, harvesters and squatters sought access to Yaquina Bay while federal agents attempted to exclude unauthorized settlers. Commercial demand for oysters linked the bay to San Francisco markets. This account connects land opening with economic and political pressure, rather than portraying removal as an isolated administrative adjustment. Its setting encompasses several coastal peoples, including Alsea and Yaquina communities.

claimBlocks.suggestedSection: Reading testimony from the shared reservation system
claimBlocks.text: In Lewis's abridged presentation of 1931 claims testimony, Annie Peterson identifies herself as Coos and recalls hardship at Yahaats and assistance from Siuslaw people afterward. Other witnesses describe work, inadequate provisions and movement between communities. These accounts help readers understand the wider Alsea reservation system. Their named community affiliations and differing firsthand knowledge should remain visible; they cannot be silently converted into testimony about every Alsea family's experience.

claimBlocks.suggestedSection: How consolidation was argued in Congress
claimBlocks.text: The February 1875 Senate debate presents a proposal to remove people from Alsea and Siletz reservation lands into a smaller designated area and open the remainder to settlement. Senator Mitchell justified consolidation partly by eliminating the expense of a second agent. Other senators questioned procedure and funding. This is evidence of how officials argued for the measure; it neither establishes community agreement nor substitutes for checking the subsequently enacted law.

inspections.reviewedScope: Entire main historical narrative, bibliography and update metadata; article paragraphs beginning September 1856 through descendants.
inspections.limits: 1865 congressional attribution is inaccurate; distinguish the December 21 executive order from 1875 legislation. Descendant governments listed concern all subagency peoples, not every Alsea family.

inspections.reviewedScope: Main authored essay, especially Huntington's responses, oyster trade, and Reduction of Coast reservation in 1865 paragraphs.
inspections.limits: Embedded archival images not independently transcribed/read. Acreage, jurisdictional conclusions, unrelated peoples' losses and the essay's Congress-in-1865 wording not adopted.

inspections.reviewedScope: Introductory scope/abridgment explanation and printed testimony excerpts, especially George W. Jackson, James Buchanan, Frank Drew and Annie Peterson.
inspections.limits: Original 1931 court transcript not independently read. No aggregate death rate, compensation chronology or broad legal conclusion adopted. Reader comments excluded.

inspections.reviewedScope: Printed pp. 1528–1529 (PDF pages 9–10): Mitchell proposal/rationale, funding debate and procedural disposition.
inspections.accessNotes: Web reader size-rejected 10.9 MB issue; ordinary HTTPS download and pypdf extraction succeeded. Selected relevant text actually read.
inspections.limits: OCR columns interleave; keep procedural claims narrow. The committee-stage amendment's adoption does not establish final statutory language or implementation.

suggestedSections.title: Subagency history without merging peoples
suggestedSections.instruction: Keep Alsea identity distinct from reservation residents and named Coos witnesses.

suggestedSections.title: Land reduction, resources and official priorities
suggestedSections.instruction: Distinguish 1865 executive action, 1875 congressional debate, enacted law and implementation.

researchGaps: Seek specifically Alsea family/community testimony rather than treating neighbouring Coos witness accounts as interchangeable.
The original 1875 enacted provision at 18 Stat. 446 was not inspected; the Senate debate must not be represented as the final statute.
The original 1865 order still needs a direct text/facsimile review; the actual 1875 debate identifies the earlier action as an executive order.
Other researchers retain Siletz community history, language, ODE place-name teaching and Frachtenberg editions; this packet adds no review claims for those materials.
